title: Same concept image, Meshy vs Tripo, which 3D model made it into my game as a world boss
author: Curious_Ad5417
selftext:
Im building Grauwacht, a dark fantasy idle game you play with others (guilds, raid bosses, guild castle sieges, PvP arena). It runs in the browser and on Android, and I make it alone.

For our first server wide event I needed a world boss, a long eastern style dragon with lanterns glowing through its belly. I made one concept image in ChatGPT and fed the same image to two image to 3D tools.

Meshy gave me a clean, light mesh, and the colors worked in my lighting right away. The mane came out well, but the glowing lanterns along the belly were missing and the face was softer. It is fully usable through the API, so it fits an automated pipeline.

Tripo (Max plan, HD model) came much closer to the image. Mane, horns, scales and the lantern tail are all there. The mesh is very heavy, about 1.9M faces, and the auto-rig did not work for a serpent body. In the end Tripo model went into the game, mainly because the head and face read much better from the front.

Here is what I did with the model, all scripted in Blender.

First I welded and then decimated. The mesh falls apart at texture seams, so my first attempt found a body only a few centimeters long. Merging vertices by distance fixed it, and then I decimated to 150k faces.

Then the script finds the spine. It cuts the body into 20 slices along its length and takes the center of each slice. That gives a center line from head to tail, even for a curled-up pose.

Along that line it builds one bone per slice, with weights by distance. Legs are detected separately (geometry below the body line) and get their own bones, so they can stay tucked in while flying.

Tripos color texture is bright, so in my night light the dragon looked silver. I darkened it, turned metallic off and let only the gold parts glow.

Idle, strike and death are procedural waves along the bone chain. I rendered them in Cycles at 24 fps on a rented GPU, cropped them to the union of all frames and packed them into animated WebPs, about 400 KB per loop.

As a bonus I tried Tripo Generate in Parts for a gift chest. Lid and body came out as separate pieces, but without texture, so I added the texture in a second step. In Blender I split the lid at the hinge, set the pivot there and rendered a 24-frame opening, which is now the chest animation in the game. With a text prompt the texture first swapped colors (the red ribbon came out teal), until I named every color explicitly.

How do you deal with very dense AI meshes before rigging? Decimate, retopo tools, or something else?

AI disclosure. The concept image is by ChatGPT, the 3D models are by Meshy and Tripo, and the code was written with Claude. The animation setup and the game design are mine.

If you want to fight him yourself, Nocthyr is the boss of our first server wide event, Lantern Night, from 6 to 11 November. Every castle on the server fights the same dragon and everyone who joins shares the reward, so every extra player helps. Its free, runs in the browser without an install, and on Android. Joining a guild before the event is a good idea. [https://grauwacht.com/start?von=reddit-aig4](https://grauwacht.com/start?von=reddit-aig4)

comments.author: Opening_Wafer_6584
comments.body:
Alex here from Tripo. This is an excellent breakdown, especially because you documented both where Tripo won and where the workflow became difficult.

The fact that you chose the Tripo model because the head, face, mane, horns, scales, and lantern details read better is great to hear. At the same time, the 1.9M-face mesh, seam-related welding issue, and auto-rig failing on the serpent body are exactly the kind of production details that are useful for us to understand.

Your scripted spine solution is especially clever.

For dense meshes, your approach of welding first and then decimating makes sense for this kind of asset. For something this long and deformable, I’d generally prioritize preserving silhouette and deformation-critical areas before worrying about getting the mesh as light as possible.

I’d also be very interested in taking a closer look at the original Tripo output and your optimized version if you’re open to sharing them.
